rows: The German rotor cipher machine goes on sale; the military adopts it later in the decade.
Bletchley Park’s codebreaking machine, the first programmable electronic digital computer.
The first general-purpose electronic computer runs its first job: a thermonuclear-weapon calculation for Los Alamos.
The Los Alamos computer runs calculations for the hydrogen bomb.
The larger model of Curt Herzstark’s handheld mechanical calculator.
In his farewell address, Eisenhower warns against the unwarranted influence of the military–industrial complex.
Unix time counts seconds from 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970.
Atari’s cartridge console brings arcade games home.
Trade liberalization and freer capital flows expand worldwide.
Namco’s maze game becomes the best-known arcade game of all time.
Peacetime defense spending rises sharply through the decade.
The Fed raises rates to about 20% to break inflation.
IBM’s open-architecture PC makes the personal computer a business standard.
Sinclair’s low-cost home computer brings programming to a generation in the UK.
The sequel, first built as an unauthorized enhancement, outsells the original in the US.
West Midlands Ms. Pac-Man champion, October 1982.
Dial-up bulletin boards form the first online communities.
Reagan proposes a space-based missile shield, nicknamed “Star Wars”.
Richard Stallman announces a free Unix-like operating system.
The Bell System is split into regional operating companies.
Apple’s Macintosh brings the mouse and graphical interface to the mass market.
Excel ships for the Macintosh; the Windows version follows in 1987.
Cfront 1.0 and Stroustrup’s book make C++ commercially available.
Windows 1.0 brings a graphical shell to MS-DOS.
Honda begins the walking-robot program that leads to ASIMO.
VSEL (Vickers Shipbuilding and Engineering), Trident launch, September 1986.
Commodore’s multimedia home computer, with custom graphics and sound chips.
The Dow falls 22.6% in a single day.
Zenith Data Systems’ line of IBM PC compatible laptops, sold from 1988 to 1993.
The border opens and the Cold War division of Europe ends.
Groupware for email and shared documents, replicated across offices.
The Nikkei peaks before decades of stagnation.
Workloads move off mainframes to Unix servers and SQL databases.
Precision-guided munitions are shown on live television.
Tim Berners-Lee publishes the first website at CERN.
Linus Torvalds releases the Linux kernel.
Spun out of MIT to build dynamically balanced legged robots.
The Pentagon urges contractors to consolidate after the Cold War.
Jerry Yang and David Filo start a hand-built directory of the web, which grows into its leading portal.
The Netscape Navigator browser brings the web to the mainstream.
Sony’s PlayStation launches in Japan, bringing 3D games to the living room.
The internet opens to commerce and investment pours into web companies.
Sun announces Java: write once, run anywhere.
Netscape ships JavaScript, making web pages programmable.
DEC launches the first full-text search engine of the web; within two years it serves 80 million queries a day.
Shields online platforms from liability for what their users post.
Senior Engineer, Advanced Development Group, Mar 1996 – May 1997.
IBM’s chess computer defeats the world champion in a match.
Filming Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace, June 1997.
Britain hands Hong Kong to China under “one country, two systems”.
Consolidation leaves a handful of prime defense contractors.
Fiction: in Terminator 2, Skynet becomes self-aware on August 29, 1997.
The term is coined and Netscape releases its browser’s source code.
Antitrust case over bundling Internet Explorer with Windows.
Equinix is founded to run neutral data centers where networks interconnect.
Google incorporates and launches its PageRank search engine.
The Fed brokers a rescue of the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management.
The online pet store launches; its sock-puppet ads made it the emblem of the dot-com bubble, and it shut down two years later.
RIM’s BlackBerry brings push email to mobile devices.
Salesforce launches, selling software as a hosted subscription.
Gramm–Leach–Bliley lets commercial and investment banks combine.
The Nasdaq falls almost 80% from its peak by 2002.
Honda unveils ASIMO, a walking humanoid robot.
Leaves credit default swaps largely unregulated.
Terrorist attacks on New York and Washington.
The US invades Afghanistan; armed Predator drones see combat.
Apple’s music player, a step toward the iPhone.
iRobot’s vacuum becomes the first mass-market home robot.
Palantir is founded to build data analysis software for intelligence agencies.
Google launches Gmail with a gigabyte of free storage.
The term names a web of platforms and user-generated content.
Google publishes MapReduce for processing data across clusters.
Boston Dynamics’ DARPA-funded quadruped walks over rough terrain.
YouTube launches video sharing for anyone.
Linus Torvalds writes Git to manage Linux kernel development.
Amazon launches S3 and EC2, starting the public cloud.
Falcon 1’s first flight fails shortly after liftoff.
Google publishes BigTable, the model for a generation of NoSQL stores.
An open-source MapReduce and distributed file system, built after Google’s papers, that brings big data to everyone.
Apple’s iPhone starts the touchscreen smartphone era.
General-purpose programming on GPUs, later the engine of deep learning.
Google’s hosted app platform, the start of Google Cloud.
Apple opens the iPhone to third-party apps.
Mortgage and credit default swap losses trigger a global crisis.
Android 1.0 ships on the HTC Dream, Google’s open answer to the iPhone.
Google’s browser, with the V8 JavaScript engine.
Falcon 1’s fourth flight is SpaceX’s first success: the first privately developed liquid-fuelled rocket to reach orbit.
Congress commits $700B to stabilize the banks.
The Fed starts buying assets at scale.
Uber is founded, popularizing the on-demand gig economy.
JavaScript on the server, built on V8.
The Supreme Court allows unlimited independent political spending by corporations.
US markets plunge and recover within minutes.
Post-crisis reform of US financial regulation.
China overtakes Japan as the world’s second-largest economy by nominal GDP.
Cloudflare launches its CDN and security network.
Jeff Dean, Greg Corrado and Andrew Ng start Google’s deep learning research team.
IBM’s question-answering system beats the show’s champions.
Conflict-free replicated data types are formalized for sync without coordination.
Amazon acquires Kiva’s warehouse robots for $775M.
A convolutional network wins ImageNet, launching modern deep learning.
The first YouTube video to pass a billion views.
Amazon wins a $600M contract to build a cloud for the CIA.
Containers become a standard way to package and ship software.
Facebook open-sources its component UI library.
Edward Snowden reveals NSA mass surveillance, including PRISM access to internet companies.
Boston Dynamics unveils the Atlas humanoid for DARPA.
One of a string of robotics acquisitions by Google.
Google buys the London AI lab for a reported $500M or more.
Generative adversarial networks pit a generator against a discriminator.
The Pentagon bets on AI and autonomy to keep its edge.
Discord launches voice and chat communities.
A Falcon 9 first stage lands upright after an orbital launch, the start of reusable boosters.
A non-profit AI lab launches with $1B in pledges from backers including Sam Altman and Elon Musk.
DeepMind’s program wins at Go, a decade ahead of expectations.
The UK votes to leave the European Union.
Donald Trump wins the US presidency.
Anduril is founded to build autonomous defense systems.
WikiLeaks publishes CIA hacking tools and techniques.
The Pentagon applies machine learning to drone footage.
“Attention Is All You Need” introduces the transformer architecture.
DeepMind’s program masters chess, shogi and Go from self-play alone, with no human games.
Data on up to 87 million Facebook users was harvested for political targeting.
Mark Zuckerberg testifies to Congress after Cambridge Analytica.
The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation sets strict rules on personal data, with fines of up to 4% of global revenue.
Google declines to renew the contract after employee protests.
OpenAI shows that generative pre-training of a transformer transfers to many language tasks.
Tariffs escalate between the two largest economies.
The European Commission fines Google €4.34 billion for tying its apps to Android, the largest EU antitrust fine.
OpenAI’s 1.5B-parameter model writes fluent text; its release is staged over misuse concerns.
The Pentagon awards a $10B cloud contract to Microsoft; it is later canceled.
The W3C standardizes verifiable credentials for self-sovereign identity.
A global pandemic shuts down economies and accelerates remote work.
The Fed buys corporate debt for the first time.
DeepMind’s agent is the first to beat the human benchmark on all 57 Atari games.
Boston Dynamics’ Spot quadruped goes on sale.
A 175B-parameter model, offered through an API, does new tasks from a few examples.
Denoising diffusion (DDPM) makes generating images by reversing added noise practical; the idea dates to 2015.
Antitrust suit over Google’s search monopoly.
Tesla releases its “Full Self-Driving” beta to a first group of owners; drivers must still supervise.
Apple moves the Mac to its own ARM chips.
DeepMind predicts protein structures at experimental accuracy.
Antitrust suit over the Instagram and WhatsApp acquisitions.
Retail traders squeeze hedge funds shorting GameStop.
Tesla announces a humanoid robot at its AI Day.
The largest war in Europe since 1945.
The data-center GPU that trains the large language models.
Western weapons such as HIMARS and Javelin flow to Ukraine.
An open text-to-image model anyone can run.
OpenAI releases ChatGPT, tuned with reinforcement learning from human feedback.
Silicon Valley Bank fails in a fast, phone-driven bank run.
A Pentagon plan to field thousands of autonomous drones.
War follows the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel.
The board fires its CEO; staff and Microsoft push back and he is reinstated five days later.
xAI releases its Grok chatbot to X subscribers.
Boston Dynamics retires the hydraulic Atlas for an all-electric version.
A humanoid for about $16,000 puts legged robots within reach of labs and hobbyists.
Waymo opens to the public in San Francisco
Fully driverless robotaxi rides become an ordinary paid service at city scale.
A federal judge rules Google illegally maintained its search monopoly.
US debt interest passes defense spending
In fiscal 2024, interest on the federal debt costs more than the defense budget for the first time.
The launch tower’s arms catch a returning Super Heavy booster.
Donald Trump wins a second term.
A US missile-defense shield is ordered.
Biden’s farewell address warns of a tech–industrial complex.
A $500B AI infrastructure venture is announced.
A Chinese open-weight reasoning model rivals the frontier at a fraction of the cost.
Humanoid robots run a half-marathon alongside people in Beijing.
The first US federal law regulating stablecoins, requiring them to be fully backed by dollars or short-term Treasuries.
The US government takes about a 10% stake in Intel, converting CHIPS Act grants into equity.
The Pentagon labels Anthropic a supply chain risk after the company refuses to drop limits on surveillance and autonomous weapons.
SpaceX agrees to buy Anysphere, the maker of the Cursor coding editor, for $60B in stock; the deal closes in August.
xAI launches Grok Bot in beta: always-on AI teammates, each with its own cloud computer.
Meta releases Muse, a personal agent that works on long-running tasks on a user’s behalf.
OpenAI launches Dots at DevDay: personal agents that pursue goals in the background, an answer to Muse.
Starshield links for Ukrainian forces are slowed, disrupting drone operations; reports that the order came from the White House are denied.
Major internet disruption from bot attack
Speculative: an automated attack takes down large parts of the internet.
Speculative: the US government takes ownership stakes in the largest AI companies.
